title: General and Administrative (G&A) Functions
description: General and administrative functions, such as payroll, accounting and executive oversight, are excluded from qualified research expenditures.
summary: General and administrative (G&A) functions are indirect overhead activities, such as payroll, human resources, accounting, general executive oversight, and debt financing, that sustain a business as a whole. For U.S. taxpayers claiming the R&D tax credit, these costs are excluded from Qualified Research Expenditures under IRC Section 41 and from Specified Research or Experimental expenditures under IRC Section 174.

body.text: General and administrative (G&A) functions are indirect overhead activities, such as payroll, human resources, accounting, general executive oversight, and debt financing, that sustain a business as a whole. For U.S. taxpayers claiming the R&D tax credit, these costs are excluded from Qualified Research Expenditures under IRC Section 41 and from Specified Research or Experimental expenditures under IRC Section 174.
Executive Summary and the Exclusionary Architecture of IRC Section 41
Financial Accounting Foundations Versus Tax Law Exclusion

General and Administrative (G&A) expenses encompass the indirect operating expenditures required to govern and sustain a business enterprise as a whole, existing independently of production volume, Cost of Goods Sold (COGS), and technical research and development (R&D) operations. Within standard financial accounting under United States Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (U.S. GAAP), G&A expenditures represent fixed or semi-fixed overhead obligations that do not fluctuate directly with revenue generation, unit manufacturing output, or laboratory experimentation volume. Standard corporate examples include compensation for centralized support personnel in human resources (HR), accounting, payroll, finance, legal, and general information technology (IT) administration, alongside corporate facility leases, non-manufacturing utilities, general office supplies, corporate insurance, and non-technical executive compensation. In financial reporting, operating expenditures that cannot be attributed directly to COGS or R&D default into the G&A classification on the consolidated income statement.

Under United States federal income tax law, however, the delineation between direct research expenditures and indirect G&A overhead serves as a foundational compliance boundary for the Credit for Increasing Research Activities under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41. Whereas financial accounting aggregates administrative overhead to reflect the total cost of operating a corporate entity, federal tax law constructs a strict statutory firewall to prevent general corporate overhead from migrating into tax credit calculations. Rather than subsidizing general corporate governance, IRC Section 41 restricts the calculation of the R&D tax credit exclusively to Qualified Research Expenditures (QREs). Pursuant to IRC Section 41(b)(1) and (2), QREs are narrowly constrained to specific categories of direct expenses: wages paid or incurred for qualified services (comprising the direct performance, direct supervision, or direct support of qualified research), supplies directly consumed in the conduct of qualified experimentation, certain payments for the right to use computers in the conduct of qualified research, and qualified contract research expenditures.

Treasury regulations enforce this statutory boundary by categorically excluding expenditures that are only indirectly connected to R&D activities, rendering general and administrative functions non-qualifying by definition. This statutory architecture preserves the legislative purpose of the tax incentive by directing federal subsidies strictly toward marginal expenditures incurred to resolve technological uncertainty, rather than underwriting routine enterprise governance or fixed administrative infrastructure. When taxpayers fail to reconcile financial statement cost centers with the narrower tax definitions of IRC Section 41, general ledger cost pools frequently contaminate R&D tax credit claims with indirect overhead, exposing the enterprise to substantial examination adjustments, QRE disallowances, and accuracy-related penalties.
Unification of the Exclusionary Standard Across IRC Sections 41 and 174

Tax compliance within R&D-intensive enterprises depends on accurately bifurcating activities that provide "direct support" to qualified experimentation from those that constitute "indirect G&A" overhead. Indirect G&A encompasses enterprise-wide administrative functions that benefit the corporate entity regardless of whether specific technical projects are undertaken, including processing payroll for laboratory engineers, maintaining the corporate general ledger, administering employee health and retirement benefit programs, recruiting personnel, and exercising general executive oversight over technical divisions.

This exclusionary principle operates uniformly across both the R&D tax credit regime under IRC Section 41 and the research capitalization and amortization regime under IRC Section 174. Under IRC Section 41(d)(1)(A), an activity cannot constitute qualified research for tax credit purposes unless the associated expenditures are eligible to be treated as Specified Research or Experimental (SRE) expenditures under IRC Section 174. Consequently, IRC Section 174 functions as the threshold statutory gateway for IRC Section 41 eligibility: any administrative expenditure excluded from SRE treatment under Section 174 is automatically barred from entering the QRE base under Section 41.

Interim administrative guidance issued by the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) and the Treasury Department in Notice 2023-63 (2023-39 I.R.B. 919) reinforced this statutory linkage by explicitly excluding costs incurred by functional G&A departments—specifically citing payroll, HR, and accounting—from the definition of capitalizable SRE expenditures under IRC Section 174. Because eligibility under Section 174 acts as the statutory gateway to Section 41, Notice 2023-63 solidifies a unified federal tax rule: indirect administrative department costs are neither capitalizable as SRE expenditures under Section 174 nor creditable as QREs under Section 41. Conversely, such excluded G&A expenses generally remain currently deductible as ordinary and necessary business expenses under IRC Section 162. Failure to segregate and strip out these indirect G&A costs from R&D claims constitutes a primary driver of IRS examination adjustments and QRE disallowances.
Hypothetical Worked Example: Specialty Composite Manufacturing Enterprise

To illustrate how the G&A exclusion operates in practice, consider a hypothetical specialty manufacturing enterprise developing an advanced, lightweight composite material for commercial aircraft components. Assume the division incurs $1,000,000 in total annual operating expenses distributed across five core functional expenditure pools. Within this $1,000,000 expenditure pool, direct research wages account for $450,000 (45% of the pool) and represent compensation paid to materials engineers conducting tensile strength testing and evaluating resin formulations; these wages qualify in full under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(A)(i) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(c)(1) because the engineers are directly engaged in qualified experimentation. Direct research supplies account for $150,000 (15% of the pool), representing the direct cost of raw chemical precursors and composite fibers consumed during the mixing, curing, and destructive testing of experimental prototypes, which likewise qualify in full under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(A)(ii) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(b)(1). Qualified contract research accounts for an additional $100,000 (10% of the pool) paid to third-party testing laboratories for specialized structural stress testing, qualifying as part of the gross QRE base under IRC Section 41(b)(3) prior to applying statutory contract research percentage limitations.

Conversely, the remaining $300,000 (30% of the pool) consists of indirect overhead and commercial expenses that fail the direct nexus requirement. Specifically, excluded indirect G&A expenses represent $200,000 (20% of the pool), encompassing compensation paid to corporate accounting personnel maintaining the general ledger, wages paid to HR personnel administering employee health and retirement benefit plans, and interest paid on a secured commercial loan financing the corporate headquarters. Although indispensable to the ongoing existence of the manufacturing enterprise, these administrative and financing activities lack a direct causal link to resolving technological uncertainty in composite materials and are 100% excluded ($0 creditable) under Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(b)(1), Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(c)(3)(iii), and IRS Notice 2023-63. Similarly, excluded sales and marketing expenses account for the final $100,000 (10% of the pool) and are 100% excluded ($0 creditable) under IRC Section 41(b)(1)–(2) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(b)(1), leaving exactly $700,000 in gross QREs and $300,000 in excluded non-qualifying overhead.

body.text: Statutory and Regulatory Foundations Under IRC Section 41
Positive Definition of Qualified Research Expenditures

The exclusion of G&A overhead under IRC Section 41 operates primarily through a restrictive, positive statutory definition of eligible costs rather than relying solely on negative enumerations. Under IRC Section 41(b)(1), a taxpayer's QREs are limited to the sum of "in-house research expenses" and "contract research expenses" paid or incurred during the taxable year in carrying on any trade or business of the taxpayer. IRC Section 41(b)(2)(A) further restricts in-house research expenses to three discrete statutory categories: wages paid or incurred to an employee for qualified services performed by such employee, amounts paid or incurred for supplies used in the conduct of qualified research, and, under regulations prescribed by the Secretary, amounts paid or incurred to another person for the right to use computers in the conduct of qualified research.

Because the statute enumerates only direct research inputs, expenditures lacking an immediate operational nexus to technical experimentation fall outside the statutory scope. Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(b)(1) codifies this exclusion for non-wage operating expenses, stipulating that expenditures for supplies or for the use of personal property that represent indirect research expenditures or general and administrative expenses do not qualify as in-house research expenses. Even when an administrative cost center is housed within the same physical building as an engineering laboratory, or when general office supplies are purchased on a departmental cost center code shared with research personnel, the functional nature of the expenditure governs its tax character. By requiring direct labor participation and physical consumption of supplies in experimentation, the regulatory framework prevents taxpayers from sweeping fixed corporate overhead into the credit calculation through cost-center pooling or overhead burden rates.
Categorical Exclusion of Management Functions and Techniques

Beyond restricting the types of expenditure inputs that qualify as QREs, the Internal Revenue Code categorically excludes administrative and managerial activities from the functional definition of Qualified Research Activities (QRAs). Specifically, IRC Section 41(d)(4)(D) excludes any activity relating to a "management function or technique" as well as "efficiency surveys" from qualifying for the research credit. This activity-level exclusion ensures that even if an enterprise applies systematic analysis or quantitative modeling to improve its corporate administration, the underlying activity fails the four-part test of IRC Section 41(d)(1).

Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-4(c)(4) and the IRS Audit Techniques Guide (ATG) for the Credit for Increasing Research Activities expand upon this statutory prohibition by enumerating specific administrative and organizational activities that fail to qualify as research. Under these authoritative provisions, evaluations aimed at improving operational workflows, administrative throughput, or labor productivity—such as time-and-motion studies, efficiency surveys, and management studies—are categorically non-qualifying. The regulations similarly exclude the preparation of financial data and analysis, including financial projections, corporate budgeting, cost accounting, tax planning, and financial reporting, as well as the development of general employee training programs and management organization plans.

Furthermore, management-driven modifications to production processes, such as merely rearranging workstations on an assembly line to improve workflow efficiency or reduce material handling time, remain excluded even when implemented immediately following legitimate R&D activities. These categorical exclusions reinforce the statutory mandate under IRC Section 41(d)(1)(B) and (C) that qualified research must be technological in nature—relying on the principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science—and must be intended to discover information that eliminates technical uncertainty through a process of experimentation, rather than advancing business management, corporate governance, or administrative efficiency.
Direct Technical Support Versus Indirect Functional Overhead
The Three-Pronged Legal Standard for Qualified Services

Employee compensation typically represents the single largest component of an enterprise's R&D tax credit claim—accounting for 45% of total evaluated expenses in the baseline claim model—and consequently attracts the highest level of IRS audit scrutiny regarding the boundary between technical execution and G&A overhead. Under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(B), employee wages qualify as in-house research expenses only to the extent the employee performs "qualified services," which the statute defines across three exhaustive functional categories. First, under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(B)(i) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(c)(1), an employee performs qualified services by directly engaging in the actual conduct of qualified research, which entails hands-on technical experimentation, hypothesis formulation, prototype fabrication, software coding, or laboratory testing. Second, under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(B)(ii) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(c)(2), an employee performs qualified services by engaging in the direct supervision of qualified research, which covers the immediate, first-line technical supervision of personnel conducting qualified research, such as reviewing experimental test results, approving technical specifications, reviewing software code commits or architectural schematics, troubleshooting experimental failures, and directing the scientific path of inquiry. Third, under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(B)(iii) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(c)(3), an employee performs qualified services by engaging in the direct support of qualified research, which encompasses auxiliary services that directly support individuals who are either directly engaging in or directly supervising qualified research.

Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(c)(3) imposes a strict causal threshold on this third category, explicitly stating that "direct support" does not include general and administrative services, or other services that only indirectly benefit research activities. To qualify as direct support, an auxiliary activity must maintain an immediate, traceable operational link to the physical or computational experimentation itself. Under Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(c)(3)(ii), qualifying direct support includes the services of a machinist machining a part of an experimental model, a laboratory worker caring for research animals or cleaning specialized laboratory equipment used in qualified research, a clerk compiling research data for statistical evaluation by research scientists, or a secretary typing reports describing laboratory test results. Conversely, a corporate administrative assistant booking general commercial travel for the engineering department, receptionists managing building entry, or general facility custodial staff performing routine building maintenance do not meet the direct support threshold.
Explicit Exclusion of Functional Administrative Departments

Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(c)(3)(iii) and IRS Notice 2023-63, Section 4.03(3), identify specific corporate service functions that are per se excluded from QREs as indirect G&A overhead, even when those personnel dedicate 100% of their working hours to serving an R&D division or are organizationally embedded within a research subsidiary. Payroll services—specifically the wages paid to payroll clerks and administrators for processing timecards, calculating tax withholdings, and issuing salary checks for research scientists and engineers—are definitively excluded under Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(c)(3)(iii). Human resources functions, such as the time spent by HR personnel recruiting technical talent, interviewing engineering candidates, onboarding scientists, or administering employee benefit plans for R&D staff, are similarly excluded as indirect administrative support. In the realm of accounting and finance, compensation paid to accountants, bookkeepers, and financial analysts for maintaining the general ledger, tracking R&D project budgets, preparing R&D tax credit studies, or accounting for research expenditures does not qualify. Additionally, interest paid or incurred on debt instruments used to finance R&D facilities, equipment, or operations is uniformly excluded as an indirect financial cost rather than a direct research input.

This regulatory bright line reflects a crucial doctrinal distinction: the test for "direct support" does not ask whether the research department could function without the administrative service, nor does it depend on internal cost-accounting chargebacks. Even if an accounting clerk is assigned exclusively to account for research expenses at a dedicated laboratory facility, Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(c)(3)(iii) explicitly classifies those services as non-qualifying general and administrative services because accounting for expenses does not directly facilitate the physical conduct of experimentation.
Hybrid Executive Roles and the Suder Rule

The boundary between qualified technical supervision and excluded G&A overhead becomes particularly acute when evaluating senior executives—such as Chief Executive Officers (CEOs), Chief Technology Officers (CTOs), Chief Operating Officers (COOs), and Vice Presidents of Engineering or Operations—who perform hybrid technical and managerial roles. Under Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(c)(2), "direct supervision" covers only immediate, first-line supervision of research; it explicitly does not include supervision of a supervisor or higher-level managerial oversight, strategic corporate planning, board reporting, investor relations, and financial analysis, all of which are excluded as G&A and management functions.

In the landmark decision Eric G. Suder, et al. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2014-201 (Oct. 1, 2014), the United States Tax Court established that eligibility for the R&D tax credit is governed strictly by the functional nature of the activities performed by the individual, rather than the individual's corporate title or organizational rank. In Suder, the CEO of a telecommunications technology company claimed that 75% of his compensation qualified as QREs based on his involvement in product ideation, technical design reviews, and patent development. Under the Suder rule, a C-level executive who possesses substantive technical expertise and actively engages in or directly supervises qualified research may include the specific portion of wages attributable to those technical activities in the QRE calculation.

However, Suder simultaneously reinforced a critical statutory limitation: even when an executive's technical activities qualify under IRC Section 41, the dollar amount of compensation claimed as a QRE must satisfy the reasonableness standard codified in IRC Section 174(e). Under IRC Section 174(e), research expenditures are eligible only to the extent that the amount thereof is reasonable under the circumstances. If the compensation claimed for the executive's technical services exceeds the amount that would ordinarily be paid for comparable technical and first-line supervisory services in the industry given the actual hours worked, the IRS and the courts will disallow the excessive portion as unreasonable. Consequently, hybrid executives face a dual substantiation hurdle: taxpayers must first establish a granular, activity-based time allocation separating qualified technical supervision from excluded G&A oversight, and second, demonstrate through market compensation benchmarks that the resulting wage figure is commercially reasonable for the technical duties performed.

Furthermore, taxpayers evaluating hybrid personnel must account for the statutory "substantially all" rule under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(B) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(d)(2). Under this provision, if at least 80% of an employee's services during a taxable year constitute qualified services, 100% of that employee's wages qualify as QREs. Conversely, when an employee's qualified services fall below the 80% threshold—as is almost universally true for hybrid C-level executives and senior managers who carry corporate administrative responsibilities—only the exact prorated fraction of wages directly attributable to qualified services may be included in QREs, and 100% of the remaining administrative fraction must be excluded as G&A.

To illustrate the quantitative impact of hybrid executive time allocations and the corresponding IRS examination posture, consider a hypothetical Chief Technology Officer (CTO) receiving an annual base salary of $200,000 who divides working hours between general executive administration (excluded G&A) and first-line technical supervision of software architecture and experimental code development (qualified under Suder v. For any given technical allocation percentage ptech ∈ [0, 1], the creditable QRE wage component WQRE and excluded G&A wage component WG&A are governed by the linear allocation identity (prior to applying the 80% "substantially all" rule of Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(d)(2)):
WQRE = Wtotal × ptech, WG&A = Wtotal × (1 − ptech)

body.text: Regulatory Consistency Under IRC Section 174 and IRS Notice 2023-63
Mandatory Capitalization of Specified Research or Experimental Expenditures

The enactment of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) of 2017 (Pub. L. 115-97, § 13206) fundamentally altered the federal tax accounting treatment of research costs under IRC Section 174. For decades prior to the TCJA, taxpayers could elect under former IRC Section 174(a) to immediately deduct research or experimental expenditures in the taxable year paid or incurred, creating minimal tax-timing friction between IRC Section 174 research expenses and IRC Section 162 ordinary and necessary G&A deductions. Effective for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, however, the TCJA eliminated the option to immediately deduct research expenses and mandated that taxpayers capitalize all Specified Research or Experimental (SRE) expenditures and amortize them ratably over a 5-year period for domestic research (beginning at the midpoint of the taxable year in which paid or incurred) and a 15-year period for foreign research.

This statutory shift elevated the importance of defining the precise outer boundary between capitalizable SRE expenditures under IRC Section 174 and currently deductible G&A business expenses under IRC Section 162. Whereas taxpayers claiming the IRC Section 41 credit historically had an incentive to classify ambiguous support costs as research-related, mandatory Section 174 capitalization created a countervailing tax accounting tension: classifying an expenditure as an SRE cost defers 90% of the domestic deduction in Year 1 (due to the mid-year convention on 5-year amortization), whereas classifying the expenditure as indirect G&A preserves a 100% immediate deduction under IRC Section 162. At the same time, because IRC Section 41(d)(1)(A) requires that qualified research activities for the tax credit first qualify as research expenditures under IRC Section 174, the scope of SRE expenditures under Section 174 establishes the absolute outer ceiling of potentially creditable expenditures under Section 41.
IRS Notice 2023-63 and the Bifurcation of Operational Overhead Versus G&A Departments

In September 2023, the Treasury Department and the IRS released Notice 2023-63 (2023-39 I.R.B. 919), providing comprehensive interim guidance on the identification and allocation of SRE expenditures under IRC Section 174. Section 4.03 of Notice 2023-63 codifies a sharp structural distinction between operational facility overhead that directly supports research and functional G&A department costs that only indirectly benefit research. First, Section 4.03(3) of Notice 2023-63 mandates the categorical exclusion of functional G&A departments, explicitly stating that costs paid or incurred by general and administrative (G&A) services departments or functions that only indirectly support or benefit SRE activities—specifically listing payroll, human resources, and accounting—are excluded from SRE expenditures. Second, Section 4.03(3) of Notice 2023-63 enforces the categorical exclusion of debt financing interest, excluding interest on debt incurred to finance SRE activities from capitalization under IRC Section 174 and mirroring its categorical exclusion from QREs under IRC Section 41. Third, Section 4.03(2) of Notice 2023-63 provides for the conditional inclusion of operational and facility costs under Section 174, clarifying that operational and management costs—such as facility rent, utilities, insurance, property taxes, repairs and maintenance, security, and depreciation or amortization allowances—must be capitalized as SRE expenditures under IRC Section 174 to the extent they are paid or incurred in the direct performance of or direct support of SRE activities, such as utility, depreciation, and lease costs allocable to a dedicated R&D laboratory facility.

A critical technical distinction governs the comparison of facility operational costs across IRC Sections 174 and 41. Specifically, under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(A) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(b)(1)–(2), facility rent (leases of real property), general building insurance, property taxes, security, depreciation, and general facility overhead are excluded from QREs under Section 41 even when 100% allocable to a dedicated research laboratory, and utilities are excluded from QREs unless extraordinary utilities are directly consumed in the experimentation process itself. Thus, while Notice 2023-63 completely unifies the exclusion of functional G&A departments (HR, payroll, accounting) and debt interest across both IRC Section 174 and IRC Section 41, the inclusion of facility operational costs (rent, insurance, property taxes, security, depreciation, and general utilities) applies strictly to Section 174 SRE capitalization rather than Section 41 QRE credit eligibility.

body.text: Compliance Strategy: Cost Allocation Mandates and Substantiation Standards
The Cause-and-Effect Allocation Mandate

To operationalize the boundary between includible operational support costs and excluded G&A overhead, IRS Notice 2023-63, Section 4.03(4), establishes a rigorous cost allocation standard. Taxpayers must allocate shared expenditures to SRE activities on the basis of a "cause-and-effect relationship" between the costs incurred and the research activities, or through an alternative methodology that "reasonably relates the costs to the benefits provided" to the research activities. Furthermore, whatever allocation methodology a taxpayer adopts—such as square footage for laboratory facility rent and utilities, or dedicated server utilization metrics for computational infrastructure—must be applied consistently across taxable periods.

This allocation framework mirrors the facts-and-circumstances compliance burden of the Uniform Capitalization (UNICAP) rules under IRC Section 263A. In practice, shared corporate service centers—such as centralized IT infrastructure or facility operations—simultaneously generate includible direct research support costs (such as dedicated lab server administration or specialized cleanroom maintenance) and excluded G&A costs (such as enterprise email, financial ERP hosting, and payroll network maintenance). Because Notice 2023-63 did not provide simplified numerical safe harbors or de minimis allocation thresholds for G&A service departments, taxpayers must conduct granular functional cost studies for each shared cost pool to prove that indirect G&A overhead has been fully removed. For middle-market enterprises with highly integrated technical and administrative operations, the administrative expense of executing bespoke cause-and-effect allocation studies imposes a substantial compliance burden that can materially erode the net economic benefit of the R&D tax credit.
Three-Step Audit Defense and Substantiation Protocol

Sustaining R&D tax credit claims and Section 174 cost allocations against IRS examination requires an evidence-based compliance workflow anchored on three operational pillars: functional activity mapping, contemporaneous time and invoice tracking, and preservation of technical nexus artifacts.

First, because tax qualification depends on the functional nature of the activity performed rather than the employee's corporate title under Suder v. Commissioner, taxpayers must conduct structured functional reviews through employee interviews and workflow mapping to link daily tasks to specific R&D projects. For shared service departments and hybrid executives, every claimed function must be evaluated against the strict direct supervision and direct support definitions of Treasury Regulation Section 1.41-2(c). Any time attributable to high-level corporate management, budgeting, personnel evaluations, or general administration must be systematically carved out prior to computing QREs.

Second, rather than relying on retrospective year-end percentage estimates—which face heightened skepticism during IRS examinations—taxpayers must implement contemporaneous time-tracking and project-accounting mechanisms. Utilizing engineering project management logs (such as Jira ticket histories), version-control code commit records, laboratory notebooks, and detailed calendar logs allows taxpayers to prove participation in technical design reviews and experimental troubleshooting as opposed to corporate board or administrative meetings. For non-wage expenditures, accounting systems must link purchase invoices for consumable prototype materials directly to specific R&D project codes while formally segregating non-qualifying general office supplies, administrative overhead, and depreciable capital equipment or general-purpose software.

Third, to substantiate the causal nexus between hybrid executive wages and technical experimentation, taxpayers must preserve contemporaneous documentary artifacts—including architectural schematics, experimental test sign-offs, engineering meeting minutes, patent drafts, and technical specification reviews—demonstrating direct technical contribution and satisfying the IRC Section 174(e) reasonableness standard. Maintaining an audit-ready file linking each hybrid executive's claimed hours to tangible engineering deliverables prevents examination teams from recharacterizing technical supervision as excluded general management under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(D).
Strategic Conclusions and Policy Recommendations for Regulatory Clarification

While the foundational legal rule that indirect G&A expenses are excluded from both IRC Section 41 QREs and IRC Section 174 SRE expenditures is well established across statutes, Treasury regulations, and IRS administrative guidance, the absence of bright-line administrative safe harbors continues to generate substantial compliance friction and examination controversy. To strengthen regulatory predictability and reduce disproportionate compliance costs without weakening the statutory prohibition against subsidizing corporate overhead, three targeted administrative reforms are warranted.
Implementation of Simplified G&A Allocation Safe Harbors (SGASH)

The Treasury Department and the IRS should promulgate Simplified G&A Allocation Safe Harbors (SGASH) within the final IRC Section 174 and Section 41 regulations. Under an SGASH framework, taxpayers meeting specified gross receipts or research expense thresholds could elect to apply a standardized, formulaic exclusion percentage or simplified headcount/square-footage allocation ratio to strip indirect administrative costs out of mixed shared service departments (such as mixed IT, facility operations, HR, payroll, and accounting), thereby eliminating the need to perform expensive UNICAP-style cause-and-effect functional studies for routine administrative cost centers.
Prescriptive Treasury Regulation Updates for Hybrid Executive Roles

Although judicial precedent in Suder v. Commissioner confirmed that C-level executives and senior managers may qualify to the extent they perform or directly supervise qualified research, existing Treasury regulations under Section 1.41-2(c)(2) provide limited objective criteria for separating first-line technical supervision from general executive oversight. Updated Treasury regulations should establish explicit, non-exhaustive regulatory examples delineating non-qualifying management functions under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(D) (such as corporate capital budgeting, investor relations, commercial pricing strategy, and strategic M&A evaluation) from qualifying direct technical supervision (such as reviewing experimental test protocols, resolving architectural bottlenecks, and approving technical design specifications), paired with safe-harbor documentation standards for substantiating IRC Section 174(e) wage reasonableness.
Formal Cross-Integration of Section 174 G&A Definitions into Section 41 Regulations

Currently, the most detailed administrative enumeration of excluded G&A department costs resides in IRS Notice 2023-63, which serves as interim guidance for IRC Section 174 capitalization rather than authoritative regulation under IRC Section 41. Relying on an interim Section 174 notice to govern Section 41 tax credit examinations creates unnecessary legal ambiguity. The Treasury Department and the IRS should formally amend the Treasury regulations under IRC Section 41 to incorporate and cross-reference the functional G&A department exclusions promulgated under Section 174, while explicitly codifying a cross-reference table that clarifies the divergent statutory treatment of facility operational costs—such as laboratory rent, building insurance, depreciation, and general utilities—between Section 174 SRE capitalization and Section 41 QRE credit eligibility.
